name: Jabêm
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Ross, Malcolm. 2002. Jabêm. In John Lynch, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley (eds.), The Oceanic Languages, 270-296. Richmond: Curzon.
catalog_locator: p. 272, §1.2 'Phonotactics, vowel harmony, tone harmony, consonant harmony and stress' (the stress sentence is the last sentence of the paragraph beginning 'Within the word, the foot plays a role in Jabêm phonology'). Tone statements: pp. 272 and 274; word/compound definition p. 272.
catalog_quote: Within the word, the foot plays a role in Jabêm phonology. The foot is iambic, that is, in its full form it consists of a sequence of two syllables, the first weak, the second strong. Thus a two-syllable word consists of a full iambic foot. A single-syllable word has one foot but only a strong syllable, and a three-syllable word like /ka-seleŋ/ has two feet, the first (/ka/) with only a strong syllable, the second (/seleŋ/) a full foot. Word stress falls on the final syllable.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote located at lines 187-192 (identical text at lines 24126-24131), under the heading '1.2 Phonotactics, vowel harmony, tone harmony, consonant harmony and stress' (line 154) on the page between the running heads '272 THE GRAMMAR SKETCHES' and 'JABEM 273', i.e. p. 272 as stated. The passage reads word for word as quoted, ending 'Word stress falls on the final syllable.'; the only differences are scanned artifacts (the djvu text has /ka-seler)/ and /seler)/ where the compiler normalised to /ka-seleŋ/, /seleŋ/) and line wrapping. Surrounding section read: p. 272 first defines 'word' (stem + affix, 1-2 syllables, max 3 for prefix + disyllabic verb stem) versus 'compound' (word(s) + clitic(s)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Jabêm is a two-tone (H/L) language; within the phonological word (stem plus affix, normally 1-2 syllables, max 3), feet are iambic (weak-strong) and primary word stress is on the final syllable, i.e. the strong syllable of the last foot. Tone is a property of the foot (both syllables of a foot share tone; L is written on the strong syllable).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated as such; Ross's foot analysis implies that in the only three-syllable words (subject prefix + disyllabic stem, e.g. /ka-seleŋ/) the prefix forms a degenerate foot with its own strong syllable, but no secondary stress is named. Streicher 1982 uses 'secondary accent' once in a dictionary entry (geleŋŋa) in the sense of tone, not stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None in Ross 2002. Contradicting older statements: Zahn 1922 as quoted in Streicher 1982: x says 'In Jabem we have no accent (stress), but a distinct pitch' and that the dictionary's accents are pitch, not stress accents; Schellong 1890: 16-18 calls word accent 'schwankend' (fluctuating) and says suffixes -gä/-geng/-ging/-ö shift it to the penultimate syllable; Schmidt 1901: 5 says nothing certain can be derived from Schellong's inconsistent marks. Dempwolff 1939 (the foundational description) could not be opened.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological 'word' (stem + affix) as opposed to the 'compound' (word(s) + clitic(s)); Ross explicitly restricts the statement to the word in that sense. Citation forms; no phrase-level statement beyond Streicher/Zahn's remark that the voice drops slightly on the last word or syllable of a sentence.
new_statements.identity_note: Ross 2002 describes standardised modern Jabêm (yabe1254), based on work with a speaker from Kwalansam village; he states there is no significant dialect variation. Schellong 1890 and Schmidt 1901 describe the pre-mission Finschhafen-area 'Jabim' of the 1880s-90s (same language, pre-tonal analysis). No separate glottocode involved.

tone_statements.citation: Hansson, Gunnar Ólafur & Allie Entwistle. 2013. Consonant stricture harmony in Yabem: manner assimilation at a distance. In Shan Luo (ed.), Actes du Congrès de l'ACL 2013 / 2013 CLA Conference Proceedings. Association canadienne de linguistique / Canadian Linguistic Association. 15 pp.
tone_statements.quote: The consonant and vowel inventories of Yabem are as shown in (2) on the next page. In addition, the language has a tonal contrast between high- and low-toned syllables. ... Perhaps the most unusual aspect of Yabem phonology is the fact that voicing in obstruents is entirely predictable based on tone (Poser 1981, Ross 1993, Hansson 2004). Stops are voiceless in high-toned syllables, voiced in low-toned syllables; contrast [ɡà-dèŋ] ‘I move towards (realis)’ with [ká-tɛ́ŋ] ‘I ask (realis)’. ... Furthermore, there is tone spreading within the two final syllables of the word
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2.2 'Yabem phonology and morphology: the basics', pp. 3-4
tone_statements.summary: High/low tone on syllables; stop voicing follows tone; tone spreads in final two syllables, prefixes high by default (so 'stem or root'). Floating item is [+nasal], not a tone. >=30 forms. No stress.

tone_statements.citation: Hansson, Gunnar Ólafur. 2004 [publ. 2005]. Long-distance voicing agreement: an evolutionary perspective. In Marc Ettlinger, Nicholas Fleischer & Mischa Park-Doob (eds.), Proceedings of the 30th Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society (BLS 30), 130-141. Berkeley, CA: Berkeley Linguistics Society. doi:10.3765/bls.v30i1.946
tone_statements.quote: The clearest case of tone-induced voicing is that of Yabem (Oceanic, Papua New Guinea; see Hansson 2004 for details and references). In this language, a lexical tone contrast (/áwé/ ‘outside’ vs. /àwè/ ‘woman’) goes hand in hand with voicing in obstruents, if any are present; obstruents are voiced in low-toned syllables, else voiceless (/típ/ ‘all at once’ vs. /dìb/ ‘thud’). The dependence of obstruent voicing on tone, combined with a tone spreading process, results in prefixes agreeing in tone and voicing with a following root ...
tone_statements.locator: p. 132, sec. 1.1 'Analogical Reanalysis of Tone-Voicing Interaction'
tone_statements.summary: Lexical high vs low contrast; obstruents voiced in low-toned syllables; tone spreading makes prefixes agree with the root (ká-táŋ vs gà-dèŋ). No count, TBU or stress; details in Hansson 2004 WCCFL.

tone_statements.citation: Hansson, Gunnar Ólafur. 2004. Tone and voicing agreement in Yabem. In Vineeta Chand, Ann Kelleher, Angelo J. Rodríguez & Benjamin Schmeiser (eds.), WCCFL 23: Proceedings of the 23rd West Coast Conference on Formal Linguistics, 318-331. Somerville, MA: Cascadilla Press.
tone_statements.quote: Root-internally, a lexical L vs. H tone contrast is maintained in output forms in Yabem, as the minimal pairs in (6) illustrate. (6) Lexical tone contrast in roots: a. áwé ‘outside’ ólí ‘body’ -sáʔ ‘to hammer’ b. àwè ‘woman’ òlì ‘wages’ -sàʔ ‘to put on top of’ ... In disyllabic roots, the two syllables agree in tone. This is best viewed as foot-bounded tone harmony ... Prefix tone is nevertheless still predictable: always H, never L. ... In other words, H acts as the default tone in Yabem, though this fact is overtly manifested only in prefixes, and only when these stand outside the foot.
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones, H vs L, contrastive only in roots within the word-final foot; prefixes default H; stop voicing predictable from tone. OT reanalysis; data credited to Dempwolff 1939, Ross. 70+ forms.

tone_statements.citation: Lynch, John and Ross, Malcolm and Crowley, Terry (2002). A grammar sketch of Jabêm. In The Oceanic Languages.
tone_statements.quote: Within the word, the foot plays a role in Jabem phonology. The foot is iambic, that is, in its full form it consists of a sequence of two syllables, the first weak, the second strong. Thus a two-syllable word consists of a full iambic foot. A single-syllable word has one foot but only a strong syllable, and a three-syllable word like /ka-seleŋ/ has two feet, the first (/ka/) with only a strong syllable, the second (/seleŋ/) a full foot. Word stress falls on the final syllable. [...] Jabem has two tones, high and low, described below. [...] The two syllables of a foot have like tone. Tone is either high or low, labelled H and L in the text of this sketch. Tone also determines the voicing of stops. In an H foot any stops are voiceless; in an L foot voiced.

tone_statements.citation: Bradshaw, Joel and Rehg, Kenneth (2001). Issues in Austronesian morphology: a focusschrift for Byron W. Bender. Canberra: Australian Natl. Univ. vii+287 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Jabem and its closest relative, Bukawa (and possibly also Kela), have developed high-low (H-L) tone contrasts fairly recently in their history (see Bradshaw 1979, Capell 1949, Ross 1993). All syllables of morphemes containing voiced obstruents (b, d, g) have predictable L tones. However, L tone is now unpredictable in morphemes where sound changes have obliterated the voicing of ancestral obstruents, as in cases where *v was lost and *z was devoiced to s. L remains the marked member of the tonal set. ... H tone is unmarked.

sources.citation: Schellong, Otto. 1890. Die Jabim-Sprache der Finschhafener Gegend (N.O. Neu-Guinea; Kaiser Wilhelmsland). Leipzig: Wilhelm Friedrich.
sources.note: Lautlehre, pp. 16-18 (between the '- 16 -' and '- 19 -' page markers): 'Der Accent der Worte ist schwankend' (word accent is fluctuating), e.g. éming ei vs. bú(g)eming; with the suffixes -gä, -geng, -ging, -ö the accent moves onto the penultimate syllable (tánüm > tänúmgä); past-tense -ga causes 'Verschiebung des Accentes'. Pre-tonal, impressionistic; Schmidt 1901 judges his accent marks inconsistent.

sources.citation: Streicher, J. F. (rev. & ed.) & H. Zahn. 1982. Jabêm-English Dictionary. Pacific Linguistics C-68. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Introductory remarks 3 'The Musical Tone' (p. x), quoting Zahn 1922: 'One must distinguish very carefully between the expressions height of tone, or pitch and accent. In Jabem we have no accent (stress), but a distinct pitch.' and 'The accents on words in this dictionary are musical tone or pitch accents, not stress accents.' Also notes the voice drops slightly at the last word/syllable of a sentence (insignificant).

sources.citation: Schmidt, P. Wilhelm. 1901. Die Jabim-Sprache (Deutsch-Neu-Guinea) und ihre Stellung innerhalb der melanesischen Sprachen. Wien: Carl Gerold's Sohn (Sitzungsberichte der Kais. Akademie der Wissenschaften, phil.-hist. Kl.).
sources.note: §5 'Accent' (p. 5): nothing can be learned about accent from Vetter's texts; Schellong accents every form but inconsistently, so nothing certain can be derived; Schellong's general rule that the suffixes ja, geŋ, o draw the tone onto the preceding syllable seems to hold for o (and ga) but with geŋ the accent often stays on the antepenult. No rule of its own.

(6) Lexical tone contrast in roots: a. áwé ‘outside’ ólí ‘body’ -sáʔ ‘to hammer’ b. àwè ‘woman’ òlì ‘wages’ -sàʔ ‘to put on top of’ ... In disyllabic roots, the two syllables agree in tone. This is best viewed as foot-bounded tone harmony ... Prefix tone is nevertheless still predictable: always H, never L. ... In other words, H acts as the default tone in Yabem, though this fact is overtly manifested only in prefixes, and only when these stand outside the foot.
